CPSC 68000 · Week 4, Part 23/24
Part C

One structure for every case

Your assignment uses the same eight headings

  1. Target and process
  2. Route in, in general terms
  3. How the control network was reached
  4. Effect on the process
  5. How it was concealed or detected
  6. Impact in CIA terms
  7. Which Purdue boundary and defense in depth layer failed
  8. What changed afterward
CPSC 68000 · Week 4, Part 24/24
Part C

A note on evidence

  • Public reports only: government alerts, incident response firms, vendors, researchers
  • Facts stated plainly. Attribution stated as attribution. Unknowns stated as unknown
  • Mechanisms at the level needed to understand the failed control, not to reproduce an attack

CPSC 68000 · Week 4, Part 26/24
Part C · Case 1

Stuxnet: what it did, how it hid

Reached the controllers through

  • The engineering workstation: the one machine with program level access (Week 3)

Effect

  • Only controllers matching one target configuration
  • Centrifuges driven out of range for short periods over weeks: wear and failures

Concealed

  • Workstation showed the original program
  • Plant screens showed replayed normal readings

Detected

  • June 2010, by an antivirus firm, from rebooting Windows machines. A side effect
CPSC 68000 · Week 4, Part 27/24
Part C · Case 1

Stuxnet: failed controls and legacy

  • CIAIntegrity of logic and of reported values, to attack availability
  • PurdueLevel 2 to 1, through the engineering workstation
  • LayersHost, application, physical control of media
  • Proved malware can damage a process through a controller
  • Controller logic cannot be verified from a compromised workstation; later generations added integrity protection
  • Attribution to the US and Israel: widely reported, never officially confirmed

CPSC 68000 · Week 4, Part 29/24
Part C · Case 2

Ukraine 2015: outage, then sabotage of recovery

Reached the control network through

  • The utilities' own remote access, stolen credentials, one factor only

Effect

  • Operators watched their HMIs open breakers
  • About 30 substations; about 225,000 customers; one to six hours

Made hard to undo

  • Workstations wiped
  • Serial to Ethernet device firmware overwritten at substations
  • Control center backup power turned off
  • Call centers flooded

Detected

  • At once, by the effect
CPSC 68000 · Week 4, Part 210/24
Part C · Case 2

Ukraine 2015: failed controls and what saved the day

  • CIAAvailability, through unauthorized commands, plus destruction of the means of recovery
  • PurdueBusiness to control to HMIs, no segmentation, single factor remote access
  • LayersPeople (phishing) and perimeter (no second factor, Week 2's highest value control)
  • Saved the dayManual operation. Crews closed breakers by hand
  • The first confirmed cyber attack to cause a power outage
CPSC 68000 · Week 4, Part 211/24
Part C · Case 2

Ukraine, chapter two: December 17, 2016 (Industroyer)

  • A transmission substation serving Kyiv; about one hour
  • Tooling built for the jobSpoke the grid's own protocols and issued commands itself; no hijacked HMI. A module against protective relays, and a wiper
  • Week 3 at scale: an unauthenticated protocol carries out any correctly formed commandThe Week 3 lab event is the same idea in miniature
  • Industroyer2, 2022: a later variant, reported detected and blocked

Case 3. TRITON (2017)

The safety system was reachable like everything else

Purdue model: TRITON acted at levels 4, 3, 2 and 1
LevelNameAttack acted here
5Enterprise, internetno
4Businessyes
3.5DMZno
3Site operationsyes
2Supervisory (HMI, EWS)yes
1Control (PLC, RTU, SIS)yes
0Processno
  • TargetA petrochemical plant, reported to be in Saudi Arabia: its safety instrumented system (Triconex). The SIS has one job: bring the process to a safe state (Week 3 Part C)
  • Route inIT to the engineering workstation that configures the safety controllers

Shaded: IT, through the control environment, to the safety engineering workstation and SIS.

CPSC 68000 · Week 4, Part 213/24
Part C · Case 3

TRITON: what was attempted, how it was caught

At the safety engineering workstation

  • A framework speaking the controllers' engineering protocol, to change the safety logic
  • Controllers left in the mode that permits programming

Effect and detection

  • No physical release
  • Twice, the safety controllers tripped the plant to a safe state
  • The second trip triggered the investigation
  • Caught by the attackers' own error, not by anyone watching
CPSC 68000 · Week 4, Part 214/24
Part C · Case 3

TRITON: failed controls and legacy

  • CIAIntegrity of the safety function, which protects human safety above all
  • PurdueThe SIS was not in its own zone with its own conduit
  • LayersArchitecture, configuration (program mode), host (the safety workstation)
  • Intent, as the reports read itDisable the protection so a later unsafe condition goes uncaught
  • Publicly attributed to a Russian research institution
  • The SIS must be independent in network terms; program mode is a physical control

CPSC 68000 · Week 4, Part 216/24
Part C · Case 4

Colonial Pipeline: the shutdown decision

What happened

  • Ransomware encrypted business systems; data stolen
  • The company shut the pipeline itself, for six days

Why

  • Billing ran on the encrypted network
  • Could not be sure OT was untouched

Effect

  • Fuel shortages across the southeastern US
  • About 75 bitcoin paid; DOJ recovered a large part

CIA

  • Confidentiality and availability on IT; physical availability loss through dependency
CPSC 68000 · Week 4, Part 217/24
Part C · Case 4

Colonial Pipeline: failed controls and legacy

  • The business to control boundary held. OT was not hit
  • But losing IT meant stopping the pipeline. The inverse of the other cases
  • LayersPerimeter (dormant account, no second factor) and policy (account lifecycle; no plan to run OT when IT is down)
  • Led to the TSA pipeline security directives of 2021 (Week 2)
  • The convergence problem in one incident: no controller touched, process stopped

CPSC 68000 · Week 4, Part 219/24
Part C

Four patterns

01

The engineering workstation or remote access, in every case whose path is documented

Weeks 6 and 7

02

Every network borne entry began in IT, a vendor, or a stray account

Stuxnet excepted: an air gap, crossed by removable media. Segmentation (Week 6)

03

The protocol never refused a command

Week 3 Part D, confirmed four times

04

Detection by effect, not by monitoring

No in plant monitoring raised the first alarm, because there was none. Week 7

CPSC 68000 · Week 4, Part 221/24
Part D

Nine stages

One shape, all four cases, in the order ATT&CK for ICS uses. A lens for reading incidents, not a procedure

Nine stages of an OT attack
StageName
1Get in
2Run code and stay
3Learn the environment
4Move toward control
5Collect process info
6Keep a channel open
7Blind the responders
8Change the process
9Cause the effect

Next week: each stage gets a name, each action a technique with an identifier, who has used it, and the mitigation that stops it. The Week 3 lab event sits at stage 8

CPSC 68000 · Week 4, Part 222/24
Part D

Each stage, and the case that shows it best

StageClearest case
1. Get in, never at the controller firstPhishing (Ukraine); dormant account (Colonial); removable media (Stuxnet)
2. Run code and stayMonths of dwell time before Ukraine 2015
3. Learn the environmentStuxnet's check for one specific controller configuration
4. Move toward controlEngineering workstation (Stuxnet, TRITON); remote path to HMIs (Ukraine)
5. Collect process informationStuxnet recording normal readings
6. Keep a channel openIndustroyer's own protocol modules
7. Blind the respondersThe wiper and telephone flood (Ukraine); the attempt on the safety system (TRITON)
8. Change the processBreakers (Ukraine); centrifuge speeds (Stuxnet)
9. Cause the effectOutage, damage, or a disabled safety function
CPSC 68000 · Week 4, Part 223/24

Summary

  • Stuxnet: controller logic, through the engineering workstation. Ukraine: remote access without a second factor, then unauthenticated protocols. TRITON: the safety system, not isolated. Colonial: IT ransomware that stopped the process through dependency
  • Where the attack reached OT, the protocol did not refuse and the plant found out by its effects
  • Every network borne entry came through IT or a vendor; Stuxnet crossed an air gap
  • Nine stages, one shape. Next week: MITRE ATT&CK for ICS, inside risk management
  • Week4-Assignment: Stuxnet or TRITON in the eight part structure. Week4-Quiz covers Parts A to D of the note
